docs.text: • A simple simulation in a shoebox room

docs.title: A simple simulation in a shoebox room
docs.text:
A 5 × 4 × 3 m room with a different material on its floor, walls and ceiling, two sources and two receivers, simulated with image sources and ray tracing. The definition reads the reverberation time T30 of one source and receiver and plots it per octave band. It builds the same room as the Python version, wall for wall.

Download the definition: simple_simulation_shoebox.ghx

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Room. A room drawn in Rhino would come in through a Mesh or Brep parameter; here Box 2Pt makes one from (0, 0, 0) to (5, 4, 3). Deconstruct Brep splits it into its six faces, List Item puts them in the order floor, right, front, left and back wall, ceiling, and Mesh Brep turns each into a mesh, the geometry an acoustic object takes.
  2. Materials. Four Construct Material components each take seven absorption coefficients (125 Hz to 8 kHz) and seven scattering coefficients, or one for every band. Merge lists one material per wall, in the order of the walls. A material from the library would come from Material Library instead.
  3. Acoustic objects. Acoustic Object pairs each wall with its material and name. Its role is boundary: the walls enclose the room.
  4. Sources and receivers. Two Source and two Receiver components, each with a position and a name. Both face +x, their default.
  5. Scene and simulation. Acoustic Scene collects the walls, sources and receivers and reports the room's volume (60 m³) and area (94 m²). Simulate Mono traces 10000 rays with image sources up to order 3 and air absorption; the seed 42 makes the run repeatable. It runs in the background, in the worker.
  6. Analysis. Deconstruct IR Graph picks the response from source_2 to receiver_2 (its Source and Receiver dropdowns), Analyse Impulse Response derives the room acoustic parameters, Deconstruct Parameter selects T30, and Plot 2D draws it.

The values differ slightly from the Python version's. Ray tracing is random, and the order in which each wall lists its corners changes which rays the seed draws; the differences are of the same size as those between two seeds.

The same example in Python.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
There are two ways to install compas_acoustics:

  • In Rhino 8 and Grasshopper, with the installer of a GitHub release. It installs the plugin's components and the worker, the Python environment they compute in. Choose this to work on the canvas.
  • In Python, from PyPI, to script with the package in your own environment.

The two are independent: the Grasshopper installer does not need a Python installation of your own.

docs.title: Install in Rhino 8 and Grasshopper
docs.text: The Grasshopper components are a compiled plugin, CompasAcoustics.gha, for Rhino 8 on Windows and macOS. Everything they compute runs in the worker, a Python 3.12 environment with compas_acoustics that the installer creates.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Download compas_acoustics_installer.zip from the latest release. It holds the wheel, the plugin (gha/) and compas_acoustics_installer.gh.
  2. Unzip it and open compas_acoustics_installer.gh in Grasshopper.
  3. Press Install. When the component says Restart Rhino, restart Rhino.

The components are then in the COMPAS Acoustics tab. The first installation downloads PyTorch for the worker, several GB, and takes a few minutes.

docs.title: What the installer does
docs.text:
• Copies the plugin into Grasshopper's Libraries folder, in a compas_acoustics subfolder, and removes the CPython components (.ghuser) of earlier versions from UserObjects.
  • Installs compas_acoustics into a Rhino script environment, for your own Python scripts in Rhino.
  • Creates the worker with uv under ~/.compas_acoustics/workers/ and records it in ~/.compas_acoustics/worker.json.

Installer options, the inputs of the installer component:

source Path of the .whl file in the bundle. Empty: the .whl file next to the .gh file. The plugin must be next to it, in gha/. venv Name of the Rhino script environment that gets compas_acoustics too. Empty: default. worker Ignored; the worker is always set up.

On Windows, if Grasshopper reports the plugin as blocked, unblock the files in the Libraries folder (Properties > Unblock).

docs.title: The worker
docs.text:
The worker starts with the first component that needs it (a few seconds; half a minute the first time) and stops with Rhino. Every Rhino session starts its own, on a free port of 127.0.0.1, and shares a random token with it: it answers only requests that carry the token, and exits when Rhino ends or dies.

The worker must run the same compas_acoustics version and protobuf schema as the plugin; otherwise the components say to run the installer again. To use another interpreter that has this version of compas_acoustics, set the environment variable COMPAS_ACOUSTICS_WORKER_PYTHON to its path. A Python script can use the same worker through compas_acoustics.worker.client().

The Worker component (Util panel) shows the worker's state; every component's right-click menu has Open worker log. See Troubleshooting when the worker does not start.

docs.title: Update
docs.text: Download the installer of the new release and run it as above. It replaces the plugin and the worker's compas_acoustics; restart Rhino afterwards.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
1. Close Rhino.
  2. Delete the compas_acoustics folder in Grasshopper's Libraries folder (in Grasshopper: File > Special Folders > Components Folder).
  3. Delete ~/.compas_acoustics/, which holds the worker.

docs.title: Install in Python
docs.text:
compas_acoustics needs Python 3.9 or newer; the Binaural and Ambisonics methods need 3.11 or newer. Create an environment, for example with conda:

conda create -n acoustics python=3.12
conda activate acoustics

Then install it from PyPI:

pip install compas_acoustics

To install the latest main instead, install it from the git repository:

pip install "compas_acoustics @ git+https://github.com/gramaziokohler/compas_acoustics.git"

docs.title: Binaural and ambisonics methods
docs.text:
The Binaural and Ambisonics methods share one hybrid engine (image sources, edge diffraction and a directional feedback delay network) and differ only in how they render it. They need pyFDN, spharpy and multislope, which compas_acoustics installs on Python 3.11 and newer; on Python 3.9 and 3.10 (Rhino 8's Python) it leaves them out and the methods are not available.

pyFDN brings flamo and with it PyTorch: about 0.5 GB on macOS, several GB with CUDA on Linux. Only pyFDN's training modules use it; the methods run without them.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
python -c "import compas_acoustics; print(compas_acoustics.__version__)"

Then follow the tutorial.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
To work on compas_acoustics, install it from a local clone with the "dev" requirements:

git clone https://github.com/gramaziokohler/compas_acoustics.git
cd compas_acoustics
pip install -e ".[dev]"

See Contributing to the documentation for building the documentation.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial builds a room, simulates its impulse responses, analyses them and listens to the result. Every step uses the classes of compas_acoustics.

docs.title: Build a scene
docs.text:
A Scene holds the room's surfaces, the sources and the receivers. A shoebox room is six surfaces, each an AcousticObject with its own material.

import compas_acoustics as ca

scene = ca.Scene("room")
scene.add_source(ca.Source("talker", 2, 2, 1.6))
scene.add_receiver(ca.Receiver("listener", 6, 4, 1.2, direction=[-1, -0.5, 0]))

A room drawn in Rhino can be read from an OBJ file instead, one object per OBJ group (Rhino layer): ca.AcousticObject.from_obj(path, materials={...}). examples/obj.py does this for a room with a table in it.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
Materials have absorption and scattering coefficients in seven octave bands, 125 Hz to 8 kHz. Take them from the library, or define your own.

library = ca.MaterialsLibrary()
carpet = library.material_from_name("carpet")
plaster = ca.AcousticMaterial("plaster", absorption_coefficients=0.05, scattering_coefficients=0.1)

room = ca.AcousticObjectsLibrary.shoebox_room(8, 6, 3, materials={
    "floor": carpet,
    "ceiling": plaster,
    "left_wall": plaster,
    "right_wall": plaster,
    "front_wall": plaster,
    "back_wall": plaster,
})
scene.add_acoustic_objects(room)

docs.title: Simulate
docs.text:
Every simulation method runs through scene.simulate, which returns one ImpulseResponse per source-receiver pair. Mono uses image sources and ray tracing; Binaural and Ambisonics use the hybrid engine and need Python 3.11 or newer.

mono = scene.simulate(ca.Mono(ray_tracing=True, n_rays=5000))
binaural = scene.simulate(ca.Binaural())
ambisonics = scene.simulate(ca.Ambisonics(sh_order=1))

docs.title: Analyse
docs.text:
Analyser derives the room acoustic parameters of ISO 3382 from a response: reverberation times, clarity, definition and more, per octave band.

(ir,) = mono.values()
analyser = ca.Analyser(ir)
results = analyser.analyse()
analyser.print_table()

docs.title: Auralise
docs.text:
Auraliser convolves the responses with an anechoic recording, in the format of the responses: here binaural, for headphones.

speech = ca.Defaults().ANECHOIC_SOUNDFILES_LIBRARY_PATH + "/female_speech.wav"
signal = ca.Auraliser("room", list(binaural.values()), anechoic_sounds=[speech]).convolve()

Ambisonic responses are convolved the same way and give an ambisonic (AmbiX) signal, to save as a multichannel file for a decoder elsewhere.

docs.title: Grasshopper
docs.text: The Grasshopper plugin has a component for each of these steps, in the panels Elements to Optimization of the COMPAS Acoustics category. Install it with the installer bundle (see Install in Rhino 8 and Grasshopper); the components run everything in a Python worker that starts with the first component that needs it.

scene.add_receiver(receiver_1)

docs.title: Visualise the specular rays of a ray-tracing simulation
docs.text:
This example traces specular rays from the sources of a shoebox room directly into a spotlight cone (a direction + half angle) in a single call, then keeps a single source and displays them, optionally truncated by reflection order or sound travel time.

"""Visualise the specular rays of a ray-tracing simulation.

This example traces specular rays from the sources of a shoebox room directly
into a spotlight cone (a direction + half angle) in a single call, then keeps a
single source and displays them, optionally truncated by reflection order or
sound travel time.
"""

from compas.geometry import Vector

import compas_acoustics as ca



########### create sources and receivers
source_1 = ca.Source(x=4.0, y=3.0, z=1.5, name="source_1")
source_2 = ca.Source(x=1.0, y=1.0, z=1.5, name="source_2")
receiver_1 = ca.Receiver(x=2.0, y=2.0, z=1.6, name="receiver_1")


########### create a scene
scene = ca.Scene(name="Ray Demo Scene", description="Specular ray visualisation.")
scene.add_source(source_1)
scene.add_source(source_2)
scene.add_receiver(receiver_1)


########### assign acoustic materials
concrete = ca.AcousticMaterial(name="concrete", absorption_coefficients=[0.01, 0.01, 0.02, 0.02, 0.02, 0.05, 0.05])
room = ca.AcousticObjectsLibrary.shoebox_room(length=5, width=4, height=3, materials={
    "floor": concrete,
    "left_wall": concrete,
    "front_wall": concrete,
    "right_wall": concrete,
    "back_wall": concrete,
    "ceiling": concrete,
})
scene.add_acoustic_objects(room)


########### trace the rays directly into a spotlight cone
cone_axis = Vector(-1, -1, 0)
rays = ca.RayField.from_scene(scene, n_rays=500, max_reflection_order=6, direction=cone_axis, angle=25)
print(f"Traced {len(rays)} rays into the 25 degree cone.")


########### keep only the rays from source_1
filtered = rays.filter(source=source_1)
print(f"{len(filtered)} rays emitted from source_1.")


########### display, truncated to the first 3 reflections (or use travel_time_ms=...)
filtered.display_in_viewer(scene=scene, reflection_order=3)

docs.title: Visualise coefficient-driven scattered rays of a ray-tracing simulation
docs.text:
At each reflection, extra scattered rays are spawned whose number and directions are governed by the surface scattering coefficient: a mirror-like surface spawns few rays clustered around the specular direction, while a highly diffusing surface spawns many rays spread toward the surface normal.

"""Visualise coefficient-driven scattered rays of a ray-tracing simulation.

At each reflection, extra scattered rays are spawned whose number and directions
are governed by the surface scattering coefficient: a mirror-like surface spawns
few rays clustered around the specular direction, while a highly diffusing surface
spawns many rays spread toward the surface normal.
"""

import compas_acoustics as ca



########### create a source and a receiver
source_1 = ca.Source(x=4.0, y=3.0, z=1.5, name="source_1")
receiver_1 = ca.Receiver(x=2.0, y=2.0, z=1.6, name="receiver_1")


########### create a scene
scene = ca.Scene(name="Scattered Ray Demo", description="Scattered ray visualisation.")
scene.add_source(source_1)
scene.add_receiver(receiver_1)


########### assign materials with non-zero scattering coefficients
concrete = ca.AcousticMaterial(
    name="concrete",
    absorption_coefficients=[0.01, 0.01, 0.02, 0.02, 0.02, 0.05, 0.05]
    )

diffusing = ca.AcousticMaterial(
    name="diffuser",
    absorption_coefficients=[0.1, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.3],
    scattering_coefficients=[0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.7, 0.8, 0.8],
)
room = ca.AcousticObjectsLibrary.shoebox_room(length=5, width=4, height=3, materials={
    "floor": concrete,
    "left_wall": diffusing,
    "front_wall": concrete,
    "right_wall": diffusing,
    "back_wall": diffusing,
    "ceiling": concrete,
})
scene.add_acoustic_objects(room)


########### trace the rays including scattering
rays = ca.RayField.from_scene(
    scene,
    n_rays=5,
    max_reflection_order=4,
    include_scattering=True,
    scatter_density=10,
    scatter_max_bounces=1,
    random_seed=42,
)
print(f"Traced {len(rays)} specular rays and {len(rays.scattered_rays)} scattered rays.")
rays.display_in_viewer(scene=scene, show_scattered=True, reflection_order=3)

########### keep a single ray so the scattering is easy to see
single = rays.filter(source=source_1, ray_index=44)


########### display both the specular ray and its scattered rays, in distinct styles
single.display_in_viewer(
    scene=scene,
    show_specular=True,
    show_scattered=True,
    reflection_order=3,
)

docs.text: Traced 5 specular rays and 65 scattered rays.

docs.text:
This example finds the image-source paths from the source to the receiver of a shoebox room up to second order, the same images pyroomacoustics finds, and displays the first and second order reflections.

"""Visualise the specular reflection paths of the image source method.

This example finds the image-source paths from the source to the receiver of a
shoebox room up to second order, the same images pyroomacoustics finds, and
displays the first and second order reflections.
"""

import compas_acoustics as ca


########### create a source and a receiver
source = ca.Source(x=1.5, y=1.5, z=1.6, name="source")
receiver = ca.Receiver(x=5.0, y=3.0, z=1.5, name="receiver")


########### create a scene
scene = ca.Scene(name="Specular Demo Scene", description="Specular reflection visualisation.")
scene.add_source(source)
scene.add_receiver(receiver)


########### assign acoustic materials
concrete = ca.AcousticMaterial(name="concrete", absorption_coefficients=[0.01, 0.01, 0.02, 0.02, 0.02, 0.05, 0.05])
room = ca.AcousticObjectsLibrary.shoebox_room(length=7, width=5, height=3, materials=concrete)
scene.add_acoustic_objects(room)


########### find the image-source paths up to second order
reflections = ca.SpecularReflections.from_scene(scene, 2)
for order in reflections.orders:
    paths = reflections.filter(order=order)
    print(f"order {order}: {len(paths)} paths, the first after {min(p.travel_time for p in paths):.2f} ms")


########### display the first and second order reflections
reflections.filter(order=[1, 2]).display_in_viewer(scene)
